paragraphs: The rain was heavy in late spring, and the Qingxi Stream was in flood. Along the imperial avenue before the Jiankang palace, rows of carriage lanterns shone back from the wet stones. Ox carts came slowly from the direction of Changgan and Black-Robed Lane, their curtains lowered. Wheels rolled through puddles, spraying fragrant mud. Palace attendants stood at either side of the vermilion gate with name cards in their hands, bowing now and then to guide a guest within. The guards knew by heart which family’s carriage could drive directly to the steps and which must wait in the outer gallery. They scarcely needed to see who sat inside.

Under the eaves at the far end of the imperial avenue, more than thirty others crowded together to escape the rain. Those without umbrellas held their straw capes over their heads. Those carrying petitions feared that the oiled cloth around them would leak. The youngest hid beneath the adults' sleeves. They had come from Kuaiji, Wu, and Yixing to bring complaints to Jiankang seven days earlier. The Secretariat sent them to the Censorate; the Censorate referred them to their prefectures and commanderies; the regional offices replied that the county had already decided their cases and that appeals to higher authorities were forbidden. After seven days of going from office to office, their shoes were worn through, and not one of their documents had been accepted.

Their leader, Lu Fu, was fifty-two, his back bent like a riverside willow twisted by floodwater. He had once possessed twenty-seven mu of farmland. Floods had destroyed nine, but his taxes were still assessed on the old register. The county officers had taken his last plough ox and then ordered his eldest son, already dead, to report for labor on a fortified estate. When Lu Fu reported the death, the clerk asked where his second son was. There was no second son, only a nine-year-old grandson, Lu Xiaoqi. The child was standing beside him now, his feet red with cold. Lu Fu tore off part of his straw cape to wrap them, leaving his own legs submerged below the knees.
“Is the Prince of Kuaiji really in there?” someone asked.
Lu Fu watched the lanterns. “He is. Tonight he is entertaining an envoy from Jingzhou. All the lords and ministers will be here. Perhaps one of them will be willing to look at our papers.”

Inside, a magnificent banquet was indeed in progress. Lacquered tables ran down both sides of the hall, laden with roast venison, steamed fish, honeyed plums, and fresh fruit. Strings and flutes sounded softly behind the curtains. Aloeswood incense curled upward with the charcoal smoke and drifted over jade wine cups. Sima Daozi occupied the place of honor and smiled with habitual warmth, calling nearly everyone a worthy man as he filled their cups. Wang Guobao sat close by, wearing a new jade-studded belt half an inch broader than the ritual regulations allowed. Not a single person in the hall cared to notice that extra half inch.

After two rounds of wine, Wang Guobao brought up the Northern Garrison at Jingkou. Liu Laozhi had a powerful army under him, he said, and had commanded it at Jingkou for too long. Jiankang ought to divide his forces and establish a separate imperial guard. Someone asked where the court would find the grain to maintain another army. Raise taxes in the southeast, Wang Guobao replied. A finance official said the levies had already risen last year and the people could scarcely endure them. Wang Guobao merely smiled: if there were no troops, would the people not be the ones to suffer when bandits came? A scion of another great clan added that the lowborn soldiers at Jingkou might not be willing to submit to the Secretariat. An envoy sent to inspect the army’s grain supplies, he had heard, had been openly defied by a mere captain.

Zhu Xu, sitting near the foot of the hall, heard Liu Yu’s name but said nothing. He had returned to Jiangnan barely half a month before and was not yet accustomed to the order of seats here, or to hearing people discuss the inhabitants north of the Huai as though they were a sum of tax revenue missing from the books. When Xiangyang had fallen and he had been carried captive into Qin territory, he had imagined he would weep to see Jiankang again, simply because the banners on its walls still bore the emblems of Jin.

But after he actually set foot on the imperial avenue, his thoughts often returned to the children learning their characters in the Qin guest settlements and to the farmers quarrelling across the wet fields. He did not like hearing Qin people sometimes call the southerners “Jin slaves,” nor had he forgotten that he was a minister of Jin. Yet the villages he had passed on his journey south stood half empty, and those who had left home so often wanted only one thing: for someone to accept their written account of a wrong.

The envoy from Jingzhou rose to offer a toast. Yin Zhongkan, he said, had lately expanded the river fleet and collected salt taxes solely to defend the upper Yangtze and hold back Qin soldiers. He hoped the court would show indulgence. Wang Guobao asked why those salt revenues had not been remitted to Jiankang. The envoy answered that fortifying Jiangling was enormously expensive. Only then did Sima Daozi lay down his chopsticks. “Are those the fortifications of the Jin house,” he asked slowly, “or Lord Yin’s private stronghold?”

For a moment the hall fell silent. Sweat ran down the Jingzhou envoy’s collar as he hastened to insist that Lord Yin harbored no disloyal intention. Sima Daozi smiled once more and said a feast ought not to feel like a court audience. He ordered the musicians to play again. Cups clinked anew, and the guests who had lowered their voices laughed along. But everyone remembered who had bowed his head while another spoke, and who had declined to raise a cup.

A disturbance broke out beyond the palace gate. Seeing an usher emerge, Lu Fu hurried forward with the others and raised the oiled-cloth parcel in both hands. He spoke of his son’s death on the levee, then of the ox that had been seized and the grandson now threatened with forced labor. The usher, surnamed Zhou, unfolded the petition and had read scarcely two lines before rebuking them for appealing above their rank and gathering to disturb the palace precincts. Lu Fu said they had spent seven days visiting every government office and no one would take their papers. Which door were they supposed to go to? The usher coldly ordered the guards to drive them away.

Someone in the crowd recognized an old emblem on Zhu Xu’s carriage and shouted, “General Zhu is inside! He has returned from the north. Will he not accept one petition from the people of Jin?” The cry struck the palace wall amid the rain. Those farther away might not have made out the words, but the faces of several imperial guards changed. Afraid the commotion would reach the banquet hall, the usher pressed the guards to act. Spear shafts swung down. The crowd fell back. Lu Fu went sprawling beside the steps, his oiled-cloth parcel falling into the water. He crawled after the papers, not seeing that Lu Xiaoqi had been pushed out into the middle of the road.

An ox cart arriving late turned out of a crooked lane. The driver jerked the reins, startling the ox into a sideways lunge. People scattered in both directions, only to be forced back by the soldiers. Lu Xiaoqi bent to retrieve his grandfather’s fallen straw cape, and someone stepped on his shoe, pulling it off. He managed a single cry of “Grandfather!” before it disappeared among trampling feet and cartwheels. By the time Lu Fu stumbled toward him and felt for him with trembling hands, the child’s chest no longer rose. The torn strip of straw cape once wrapped around his feet floated into the gutter like a withered stalk no one would claim.

The music had not stopped in the hall. Wang Guobao was proposing that the Northern Garrison’s pay be disbursed directly from Jiankang, lest Liu Laozhi grow independent with his troops. When the finance official asked where the funds would come from, he proposed combining old river taxes under a new heading. Someone at the tables laughed: did he think the people would not recognize a grain levy merely because its name had changed? Sima Daozi did not smile. He was about to speak when an attendant leaned to Zhu Xu’s ear and told him that some unruly peasants were shouting his name outside and demanding that he intervene.

Zhu Xu rose and asked leave to see what was happening. Sima Daozi replied that the palace gate had officials of its own. General Zhu had been away from Jiangnan for so long; why abandon the banquet over a trivial affair? Zhu Xu had no choice but to sit down, though he never touched his wine again. A little later the attendant returned, the hem of his robe stained with mud, his face white as paper.
“What happened outside?” Zhu Xu asked.
“They have dispersed.”
“Was anyone hurt?”
The attendant did not answer. Zhu Xu set down his cup and raised his voice. “What did you see?”
“A child. He’s dead.”

The base of the cup struck the table with a sharp sound. Several guests nearby turned at once. Wang Guobao said there were laws against trespassing on palace grounds. Any deaths or injuries ought to be blamed on those who had led the disorder, and with so many guests present tonight the matter should not be spread throughout the city. Zhu Xu looked at him and suddenly felt the incense was too thick in the hall, too thick to breathe. He bowed to Sima Daozi and asked to withdraw on grounds of illness. But Wang Guobao cut in, asking whether the general, after so many years at the Qin court, had forgotten his own sovereign, since he seemed so ready to speak for the northern dynasty at every turn.

Zhu Xu had been about to leave, but now he stopped. He said that after Xiangyang fell he had been taken prisoner. He had neither joined Qin armies to attack Jin nor commanded troops for the Qin court. His joy on seeing his home in Jiangnan still standing had been no less than he had imagined. Yet he had seen countless people of Jin leave their homes, while no one would ask why they went. He mentioned a woman who had once returned to Huainan to visit her ancestors' graves: she had suffered insults on the northern bank but had also succeeded in bringing a case against officials who stole grain. Now he asked the assembled lords: a family outside the palace had been stripped of its fields, and a child had died on the steps. Which of them was willing to examine that family’s original tax register even once?

Wang Guobao angrily accused him of using the laws of the foreign Qin to deride the Jin court. Zhu Xu no longer disputed the phrase “foreign Qin.” He looked only at Sima Daozi. “Prince of Kuaiji, can the petitions outside at least be received?”

Sima Daozi was silent for a moment, then rose and called Zhu Xu to accompany him into a side hall. Water lay uncleared along the corridor, and palace lanterns shone on the rain streaking banana leaves. When they reached a place beyond hearing, the prince put aside his banquet smile and asked whether Zhu Xu truly thought he did not know what was wrong in the southeastern commanderies. Powerful clans annexed land; military families lost their farms; pirates raided the coast; Jingzhou raised its own levies; the Jingkou garrison was owed its pay. Memorials piled up year after year. Investigate one magistrate and several great houses stood behind him. Send the Xie family to investigate and the Wangs would object; send the Wangs and the Huans would grow afraid. Send the Northern Garrison and the court would find it harder still to bring that army under its control.
“Did you never hear such arguments in Qin country?” Sima Daozi asked.

Zhu Xu said he had, and had also seen the Qin court change its old military order until it nearly provoked a mutiny. The prince replied that Jiangnan could not follow the north in letting a single emperor dominate every faction. Zhu Xu did not deny it. He asked only whether the death of someone outside the palace gate meant that, out of regard for the great families, the court could not even bring itself to enter a child’s name in a record.

Sima Daozi sat beneath the lamp for a long time. At last he ordered the petitions from the gate and the register of dead and injured brought inside, and forbade anyone to destroy privately the duty roster of guards stationed at the street entrance that night. Zhu Xu bowed in thanks. The prince smiled bitterly. Zhu Xu had got his one written order, he said, but tomorrow dozens of government offices would still refuse to open their doors. Zhu Xu said he knew. Someone must first carry that order and knock.

A verbal summons from the emperor arrived soon afterward. Sima Yao sat alone in an inner chamber. The wine before him remained full, but three rolls of frontier reports lay open. He was thinner than Zhu Xu remembered. When his old general entered, his first question was whether Fu Jian in Chang’an truly allowed Jin people to live under him without making them formally surrender. Yes, Zhu Xu answered. But powerful men in Qin still seized other people’s fields, and officials still abused their influence. Anyone who listened only to imperial edicts and never looked at the counties would misjudge that realm.
Sima Yao smiled at this. People in Jiangnan often made monsters of Former Qin, he said, but Zhu Xu did not. Then he asked, “If there is misrule over there as well, why do people still go north?”

“Some are merely escaping a flood or a few rounds of forced labor,” Zhu Xu said. “Some regret leaving. Some are deceived by officials there. But someone on the north bank gets a sheet of paper with his own name on it and comes back to tell relatives and friends that there is a place to complain when life becomes unbearable. That news travels faster than proclamations from the Qin army.”

The emperor closed the frontier report. A gust passed beyond the doors and the candle flames shook violently. Zhu Xu told Lu Fu’s story from the beginning: nine mu of his twenty-seven had been ruined by flooding, but his taxes were still assessed on the full holding; county officers demanded service from a dead man; the grandson had accompanied him to submit a petition and had died that very night outside the palace. Sima Yao asked who had ordered the petitioners dispersed. That remained unknown, Zhu Xu said. He requested permission to inspect the watch roster from that night and the old Kuaiji tax rolls, rather than having the petition returned yet again to the county against which it was brought.

Sima Yao paused before taking up his brush. He knew that opening a case would offend the superiors of the palace guards and meet resistance from the great families of Kuaiji. At last he ordered an attendant to bring fresh paper and wrote three directions: investigate the casualties, accept the petitions, and audit the land taxes. He instructed Zhu Xu to work with the censors in reviewing the rolls of fugitive households in Kuaiji, Wu, and Yixing. At the end, looking toward the old map of Jin, he quietly asked whether Fu Jian would come south again.

“I do not know,” Zhu Xu answered. “In Qin territory I saw how deeply he feared having his line of retreat cut off. He will not lightly send a great army toward the Fei River again. But he has not abandoned his desire to unite the realm.”

Sima Yao’s gaze settled on the line of the Huai. Only after a long while did he say, “If Jiangnan can keep its people here, then no matter how many soldiers the north bank holds, they cannot decide for those people which land is their old home.”

Zhu Xu assented and accepted the handwritten edict, its ink still damp. When he left the inner hall, the banquet guests had all dispersed. Outside the palace gate only a few soldiers remained, clearing away broken lanterns. Rain had washed the street bright, though a little patch of bloody water still marked the foot of the wall.

Lu Fu sat against the wall with Lu Xiaoqi in his arms, the boy covered by a wet cloth. Zhu Xu walked up to them. The old man slowly raised his head and asked whether General Zhu had returned from Qin. Zhu Xu said he had. Would the officials over there also drive people away from their doors, the old man asked? After a long silence Zhu Xu answered, “There are places there too that refuse to accept petitions.”
Lu Fu looked down and touched the boy’s ankle. “Do children die over there too?” he asked again.

“They do.” Zhu Xu crouched and laid the handwritten edict beside the bundle of petitions, now soaked and falling apart. “I will investigate what happened tonight. You may not get your fields back quickly. We may not quickly find the people responsible for your grandson’s death. But first his name must be written down.”

Lu Fu still gripped the petitions, as though the seven days of desperate effort would be wasted if he released them. Zhu Xu found a piece of paper that was still dry and asked the old man to speak the child’s name. His brush hesitated. In the faint light of the palace lantern, he wrote: “Lu Xiaoqi, nine years old. Grandson of Lu Fu, Kuaiji.”
The old man stared at the inked characters without weeping. He held the child a little tighter, and after a long while said softly, “Don’t lose it this time.”

Zhu Xu put away the paper and ordered his accompanying soldiers to fetch dry clothes and a wooden couch and take the grandfather and grandson to shelter. He made no grand declaration at the palace gate about restoring Jiangnan to glory. At the end of the imperial avenue, ox carts passed through the standing water, and several ministers just returned from the banquet were already discussing the next day’s appointments. One by one the lanterns disappeared into the distance. Zhu Xu looked back at the closed palace gate, then set off for the Censorate. It was time for the clerks keeping night duty there to wake up.
